articles.title: Why more women carry the 'mental load' - and how couples can share it
articles.summary: Planning, organising and remembering household tasks falls disproportionately to mothers - here are some tips to help.
articles.body:
"My head's always full," says mum-of-three Stacie Matthias. "I go to sleep with a mental to-do list."

She's talking about the concept of the "mental load" - the burden of planning, organising, remembering and anticipating tasks that keep a household running.

These tasks include: remembering school trips, checking for updates in parents' WhatsApp groups, noticing which parts of the house need cleaning, monitoring how much sleep children get, scheduling doctors' appointments and buying school uniforms.

According to academics, this is work that in heterosexual couples disproportionately falls to women - particularly mothers - alongside the bulk of physical household labour.

All relationships and households are different, of course, but studies suggest clear patterns.

Children in the UK have just gone back to school from the summer holidays, and Stacie, 37, from Stockport, says her mind often feels especially busy in September.

"It's that feeling of always having something to remember, organise or worry about that makes this time of year particularly full-on," she says.

For Stacie this list of responsibilities leaves her mind feeling like a washing-up bowl that's being filled up throughout the day.

"If someone's not helping you remove those pots and pans, your water's overflowing by the end of the day," she says, "and you're at tipping point."

In a survey looking into the mental load that involved 3,000 US parents, academics at the University of Bath and the University of Melbourne found that mothers handled 71% of household tasks that required mental effort, such as keeping track of when sheets and towels needed to be washed and remembering by when food in the fridge needed to be eaten.

The study found that fathers handled many of the tasks researchers described as "episodic" - things that happen less often, such as remembering when to get the car serviced.

University of Melbourne Prof Leah Ruppaner describes the mental load as being invisible, enduring and without boundaries. "You don't bring your dishes to work, but you bring the mental load everywhere," she says.

The mental load is a popular topic on forums like Reddit and Mumsnet, where women seek advice about how to talk to their partners about the exhaustion of trying to juggle so many different responsibilities.

Mums told BBC News they were often added to school WhatsApp groups - where parents discuss things like non-uniform days, school trips, birthdays and lost property - as the "default parent", while their partners never joined.

Sophia, a 35-year-old mum of three in Portsmouth, pays for school trips and makes lunch orders on her children's school's app on her phone, but says her husband has never downloaded it.

Sophia says she tried multiple times to explain the concept of the mental load to her husband - but feels he didn't understand and dismissed her concerns as "quick tasks".

"They are quick tasks if you could just do the task," Sophia says, "but I have to plan for the task, I have to anticipate the task, I have to be 10 steps ahead all the time."

Sam Berry, a deputy headteacher, content creator and married dad of two in London, says when his wife first raised the idea of mental load after his eldest was born, he "didn't really get it" and was "a bit defensive" because he thought he was doing a lot - changing nappies, feeding the baby and more.

He would ask what he could do to help, but he says that still puts the burden on the other person to do the thinking.

As Stacie explains: "I always say to my partner: 'If I have to ask you to do something, that's just adding to my mental load'."

It took a few months of talking and listening for Sam to understand that it was not only about completing the task, but the thinking around it - not just cooking dinner, but what food was in the house, planning the meal, and doing the shopping.

Clinical psychologist Natasha Wallace says some women come to her feeling stressed by the pressure they feel to organise their households.

"It's often, for them, not one enormous stressor," she says. "It's when they realise that they have hundreds of tiny demands on them and their brains and bodies just can't switch off."

Many women are running on autopilot, she adds, so they often don't realise the extent of the cognitive load they're carrying, and this constant low-level stress can have an effect on the nervous system. In turn, this can cause poor sleep, irritability and decision fatigue, she says.

Anita Cleare, parenting expert and author of The Work/Parent Switch, said the overall cognitive drain spills over into our work lives and leads to unsustainable burnout.

One piece of research found that men who earned more did less physical and cognitive labour related to the household, but that when women's earnings increase, they do less physical housework but still the same amount of cognitive labour.

Women very seldomly feel it is a choice to opt out of family life, so the choice then becomes whether to decelerate their career, go part-time, or stop and stay home - with more and more women making that decision, Cleare says.

"If you lower the domestic load, if you lower the mental load, you will create energy, capacity, interest in being able to perform more and better at work."

Many of the women the BBC interviewed said they believed the disparity began with maternity leave.

Wallace says that because women typically take much longer for maternity leave than dads do for paternity leave, they become the "default parent" very early on.

"If you become the person who knows everything, knows where everything is and has in the past done everything, everybody starts coming to you for everything," she says, "so you remain that central person even if you return to work."

In the UK, mothers can take up to 52 weeks of statutory maternity leave, 39 of which can be paid, while fathers can take up to two weeks of leave with statutory paternity pay. Parents can also take shared parental leave.

Some employers offer extra parental leave to their workers, but most people earn less when on maternity or paternity leave, which affects how much leave many fathers take.

Cleare says workplaces can help by making examples of fathers taking paternity leave, not just offering it, and by setting expectations around when employees are contactable, and supporting career conversations for women.

It can also come down to what are seen as traditional roles.

Zach Watson, a married father of three and coach in the US on sharing the mental load, says his grandfather might never have cooked a meal in his married life, while his father did only a little.

In the first five years of his marriage, his wife cooked most of the time. If he offered to cook, he would ask her what she wanted - a question that could actually add to her mental load.

He learned he could come to her with options for dinner, having already looked in the fridge, and give her a default if she wanted to opt entirely out of decision-making. And if he needed help, instead of just asking "Where's the ketchup?", he could explain where he had already looked.

Sam Berry says while some men do not care, a big group - his audience online - "actually are really good husbands, are really good dads, they are trying their best and want to do the best they can, but almost haven't seen it or don't have the language".

Many women the BBC spoke to were keen for their partners to take ownership of certain tasks.

Sam calls this taking on "a category of tasks" - so dad might handle all the school admin, while mum manages the food.

However, he says equality is not necessarily about splitting everything 50/50 - because one partner might work more and another might like cooking - but about finding what works best for both partners.

And if you traditionally hold more of the mental load, you might need to accept that your partner may do things very differently, and it might not always go smoothly, says Afua Williams, 40, a mother of two in London.

Those who spoke to BBC News shared their own tips about how to manage the mental load equally:

Communicate clearly with your partner about how you're feeling and the impact of your mental load. Zach calls it "labelling" - making the invisible cognitive and emotional labour visible. Don't have these conversations when you're feeling angry or overwhelmed, says Wallace, or it can feel like the other person is being "blamed or criticised"

"See what you can offload" , says Ana Catalano Weeks, co-author of a study on how mental load impacts work. Do you really need to organise physical birthday cards for your children's friends? Can you mute parents' WhatsApp groups and just focus on official school emails?

Have regular check-ins with your partner - it could be daily, weekly, or seasonally

so that everyone is aware of birthdays, school meetings and more

Take ownership of tasks from start to finish without the need to be reminded, Wallace says

Don't fall into the "efficiency trap " that the solution is just to be more organised, Cleare says. Remember that what matters most as a parent are moments of connection with your child - not eating certain vegetables - and that will help redefine expectations

articles.title: Majority Russian-speaking city in Ukraine considers language ban in the arts
articles.summary: Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa decides this week whether to ban Russian-language content in music and literature in public.
articles.body:
Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa will decide this week whether to back a controversial plan to ban the Russian language in the arts.

The proposal being considered by councillors in Odesa on the Black Sea coast aims to add to existing restrictions on Russian imposed by national legislation.

It is particularly significant because Odesa is overwhelmingly Russian-speaking, although the ban would only affect public spaces and everyday usage of Russian would remain unaffected.

For millions of Ukrainians, Russian is their first language including many of the troops defending the country in its war with Russia. But Ukrainian is the only state language and spoken by the majority, and some see Russian as a tool of Russian influence.

The proposal in Odesa, which is targeted daily by Russian drone and missile strikes, calls for a complete halt to Russian-language content in music and literature, in streets, parks, public institutions and state-run arts and entertainment venues. It would also recommend a ban in privately owned spaces.

In a city famous for Russian-language writers and musicians, it has provoked strong passions.

The ban would extend in public spaces to old Odesa songs almost universally known throughout the former Soviet Union. All Russian-language books would be removed from display in public libraries. Currently, they can be shown, but not prominently.

"The Russian language is a weapon of Russia, and we need to try to fix that," says Odesa lawyer Artem Kartashov, who has advised local authorities on an official programme to "decolonise" the city of its historic Russian legacy.

"With Russian-speaking music and other things, Russians try to deconstruct Ukrainian identity and influence especially young people, because they grow up in a Russian-speaking environment."

But comic actor Borys Barsky, one of Odesa's best-known entertainers, says: "Russian isn't [only] the language of Putin, it's the language of [writers like] Dostoyevsky and Bulgakov.

"Who benefits from setting people against other people who love Ukraine just as deeply, only love it in a different language? Only Putin benefits from this."

Russian President Vladimir Putin has often referred to what he falsely describes as repression of the Russian-speaking minority in Ukraine as one of his justifications for launching his invasion of the country.

Russian and Ukrainian are closely related, but distinct in many ways. Many in Ukraine speak a mixture of the two, known as surzhyk .

Russian is the native language of President Volodymyr Zelensky, which he used often in his election campaign but has since used only Ukrainian in public.

But a 2019 law requires use of Ukrainian in many public and professional contexts including education, public services and customer service.

Public-facing workers - including waiters, shop assistants and doctors - must address customers or patients initially in Ukrainian, though they can later switch to Russian if the client prefers that.

Odesa's Mask Theatre, run by Barsky, has been fined for infringements of the legislation including using Russian in publicity materials. A later inspection found further violations such as a cafe sign with the Russian word for coffee.

"This isn't even like Orwell or Kafka, it's just madness," he says.

Russian strikes destroy 12 million books ahead of Ukraine's first week back at school

In Odesa, no-one is safe from Russia's new Black Sea strikes

Under fire from the sea, families in Odesa try to escape Russian barrage

Barsky has been able to continue to perform in Russian because it is a private theatre.

The new language proposal - similar to one already in force in the capital Kyiv and some other cities – would urge but not require private premises including shops and cafes to adopt the ban.

Odesa's state-appointed language ombudswoman, Anna Nerush, who inspects premises to check on alleged violations of the rules, thinks if passed it will put pressure on them to comply.

"All businesses interact in one way or another with local government," she told the BBC. "They rent premises, they need advertising permits, and so on. So for many entities it's important to comply with a council decision, even if doesn't provide for sanctions for non-compliance. "

Public playing of songs by Russian citizens is already illegal across Ukraine, with exceptions for some artists who have publicly condemned the war, but Russian-language songs composed or performed by Ukrainians are still allowed.

Under the proposals they would also be banned in public places.

Anna Nerush said it would not affect someone celebrating their birthday in Russian in a private room in a restaurant, as it could not be heard outside.

"But on the streets, [hearing] the Russian language can be a real trigger, for example to [former] prisoners of war and people who've come from occupied territories," she said.

Many native Russian-speakers in Ukraine have switched to Ukrainian in recent years, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

Photographer Natalia Mykhailenko switched even earlier. She has led tours of Odesa highlighting non-Russian elements of its history.

These include landmarks such as a Cossack cemetery that dates back to before 1794. That is the year Russian empress Catherine the Great is said to have founded the city, although it has been widely questioned in recent years.

A statue of Catherine was removed from a central Odesa square after a council vote in 2022, and streets have been renamed to commemorate some Ukrainian writers and activists.

"We must understand we were a colony," said Mykhailenko. "And these [language] laws are very important. I understand it's maybe sometimes not democratic. But without it, there will be no normal Ukraine in the future."

Anthropologist Anastasia Piliavsky, part of a group called Ukrainian Cosmopolis which aims to defend freedom of thought and speech, believes Russian-speakers are being made to feel like second-class citizens who are deprived of their heritage.

"In Ukraine, the vast majority of people understand both Russian and Ukrainian. So the question is not really one of language, it's one of liberty," she said.

"Ukraine has been fighting for freedom. The point of this war is not to be under authoritarian rule. That's what Russia has to offer. So when fines, or the threat of being fired [for breaking language laws] arrives, then people start wondering: what are we fighting for?"

It is unclear how much support the new language proposal has. It is opposed by an influential group of councillors linked to former mayor Hennadiy Trukhanov.

Beyond Odesa, a national poll showed 80% support for Ukrainian dominating "all spheres of communication" in 2022. However, a more recent survey of students in Kyiv found that 82% chose to speak Russian during break times, even though Ukrainian is enforced in classrooms.

One famous Odesan who found himself at the centre of the language controversy is Pavlo Viktor, a physics teacher whose online lessons have been followed by millions around the world.

Ukrainian language campaigners criticised him for putting the videos out in Russian, his first language, although he later translated them into Ukrainian. He was later criticised for saying he would talk to scared children in Russian during missile attacks, if that was the language they preferred.

Viktor is keen to take the heat out of the argument, explaining that currently about 10% of the Odesa population spoke Ukrainian in the street: "But if we wait 50 years, maybe 90% will speak Ukrainian."

"Ukrainianisation must be polite and soft… not to persuade children to move from Russian to Ukrainian, but to make an atmosphere when they want to do this. It's the best way. And I hope that gradually we'll move in that direction."

You can hear more about the language controversy in Odesa in the Crossing Continents podcast Ukraine: Fighting Russia, Fighting Russian, available from Tuesday 8 September.

articles.title: James Bond: the 007 questions fans want answered about its future
articles.summary: Speculation has been building recently that an announcement about Daniel Craig's successor could be close.
articles.body:
James Bond is special. Playing him propels an actor into an exceptionally elite group of performers. From Sean Connery to Daniel Craig, only six people have ever played him in the official film series.

In the last decade alone the UK has had more prime ministers, and twice as many people have walked on the moon than have played the British secret agent.

The last announcement of a new Bond was 21 years ago in 2005. So it's inevitable for Bond fans to want to have their questions answered about the future of one of cinema's most sought after roles, in one of cinema's biggest franchises.

1. Who will be the next person to play 007?

This is, of course, the big question fans have been talking about for the last six years. And with an announcement edging closer and closer, the speculation has intensified recently.

Many of the same well-known faces have been bandied about for months, if not years. Those names have generally included Henry Cavill, Harris Dickinson, Jacob Elordi, Jack Lowden, James Norton, Jack O'Connell, Callum Turner and Aaron Taylor-Johnson.

More recently, other names have also been thrown into the mix.

Earlier this year Variety reported that stage actor Tom Francis had auditioned for the role. And in late August Page Six claimed there will be more auditions this month, and that Gladiator 2 star Paul Mescal and Heartstopper and SAS: Rogue Heroes star Jack Barton are also on the audition list .

The announcement about the next film's producers referred to keeping Bond's spirit alive "as he embarks on his next adventure", seemingly confirming that Bond would remain male.

However, it's never been clear whether the rumoured names have been well-sourced inside information, or merely guesswork and speculation.

Back in May, Amazon MGM Studios who now control the Bond franchise confirmed the casting process was under way . But little detail beyond that was given, the statement only saying: "While we don't plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we're excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right."

It now seems that the right time is fast approaching. In an interview with Deadline Amy Pascal, one of the next film's producers, was asked whether we might have news on who would be playing Bond by the end of the year. She replied: "I would say the end of the year is a good bet."

Last month entertainment writer Daniel Richtman said on social media: "I hear they're in the final round of casting for James Bond and might have already found their guy."

His post on X was followed up by journalist Jeff Sneider who said: "Heard the same rumour. First it was down to seven, then three. Now 'they may have found their guy'. Who knows at this point? But for some reason, I don't think it's any of the so-called frontrunners, including the Aussie…"

The Aussie is almost certainly a reference to Euphoria and Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi, who was brought up in Brisbane and Melbourne before moving to the US to pursue his acting career.

The audition process is likely to have been carried out in a similar way to previous castings.

The scene that many would-be Bonds have traditionally had to peform is taken from From Russia With Love, where 007 comes out of his bathroom to find Tatiana Romanova in his bed. It's a scene where an actor relies on their physical presence, movement and charisma. No explosions fights or gadgets.

As GoldenEye and Casino Royale director Martin Campbell explained to entertainment website Gold Derby : "The word is effortless. You never see Bond fumble, he is very economic, efficient and effortless. That scene covers all the bases, basically."

And for a series where the stakes are so high, no expense is spared in ensuring that the film team know exactly how each auditionee will come across on screen. As the 007 team themselves have explained in the past : "Bond screen tests are elaborate affairs involving hair and make-up, costumes, sets, and other actors."

Generally, the unveiling of a new Bond has taken place at a London press conference in front of the world's media. But for the first time creative control of the franchise is in the hands of a studio like Amazon MGM.

Amazon purchased MGM for $8.5bn in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond. And they're reported to have paid at least $20m more for the rights to creatively control Bond's future.

Having paid such eye-watering amounts, it seems more than possible that Amazon MGM might well wish to drive fans towards their streaming service, with any reveal of the new Bond being exclusively announced on Prime Video.

It would almost certainly see a surge in streaming subscriptions. And such an announcement would still inevitably be covered by the world's press.

Global James Bond Day on 5 October, the 64th anniversary of the release of the first film Dr No, is fast approaching. So this date might be a good day for fans to mark in their diaries for a possible announcement.

We don't yet know what it will be called, or have a confirmed release date. Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight is currently writing the script, and Dune's Denis Villeneuve will direct. They and the team may well already have a title in mind. Or, of course, they may just be calling it Bond 26 for now.

Most of the series have taken titles from the original Ian Fleming stories. Four of those remain unused - The Hildebrand Rarity, Risico, 007 in New York, and The Property of a Lady. Although elements from those stories have already been used in previous Bond films.

Fans have also been busy putting forward their own suggestions for potential titles. Since the accession of King Charles III in 2022, those suggestions have included On His Majesty's Secret Service, and King & Country.

As for a release date, it's been widely reported that the next film is likely to be released in 2028. That means it's almost certain that this will be the biggest ever gap between films, more than the six years and four months between 1989's Licence To Kill and 1995's GoldenEye.

6. How far ahead are the Bond team planning?

Only the Bond team themselves really know this.

But Amazon MGM do have the financial resources to plan well ahead, and explore various issues, such as how Bond will operate over multiple films; will there be an overriding arc that will cover his journey over the next decade etc; will there be a film every two years, every three years, every four or five?

Additionally, with such a huge investment, AmazonMGM will undoubtedly be keen to learn from Disney's experiences with Star Wars, and Marvel's experiences with its Marvel Cinematic Universe, in how best to use the Bond franchise.

While there might be appetite for multiple Bond spin-offs, eg Young Bond, the Miss Moneypenny adventures etc, they will also be wary that they don't over-saturate the market, and damage the films which are at the core of the Bond franchise.

7. How will the next film deal with the ending of the last?

The below contains spoilers for No Time To Die

Daniel Craig's farewell at the end of No Time To Die saw him on the island lair of the film's villain, Rami Malek's Safin, as it was struck by a volley of air strikes, with the super spy apparently finally meeting his demise.

Rumours have indicated that the next film might well reflect Bond's early years at the start of his MI6 career, in effect a reboot, which means that there won't be any pressure or sense of disappointment that the story won't reflect No Time To Die's conclusion.

And in any case, Bond fans have been reassured by the message that has appeared at the end of almost every Bond film - "James Bond will return".

It looks like soon we'll be finding out who that James Bond will be.

articles.title: Natalie Imbruglia on her worst audition: 'I remember feeling icky'
articles.summary: The pop star's first album since 2021 deals with the mental health fallout of perimenopause.
articles.body:
When it comes to writing music, Natalie Imbruglia needs constant motion.

"I walk around in circles to get the melodies, to catch them," the Australian singer says.

"So if I go and work with someone new and they have a shoebox-sized studio, I'm like, 'How am I going to do my circles?'"

Imbruglia doesn't know exactly how many laps she completed during the making of her dancefloor-ready seventh album, Algorithm. But it was a lot.

Inspired by Talking Heads and Grace Jones, it's a record whose shimmering surfaces disguise lyrics of deep emotional complexity.

On Who Dimmed The Lights, the 51-year-old addresses how her mental health "unravelled" as she went through perimenopause.

"It was really tough," she says. "Perimenopause is not just about hormones. It's to do with your mind. Your brain needs oestrogen to function, so when the levels fluctuate, it affects your spatial awareness.

"I've never walked into so many doorways. The brain fog's quite jarring."

Doorways weren't the only problem. Imbruglia says perimenopause exacerbated her ADHD, which she was diagnosed with in midlife. Other symptoms included heightened anxiety and anger.

"You start seeing an expression on other people of, like, 'What's happening to you?'

"I was seeing that face a lot, and it's to do with your ability to process [information]. Your fuse is shorter."

Things came to a head on tour, where her stage fright went into overdrive and she suffered "just terrible, terrible anxiety".

"I become sensitive to sound, so it feels like you're screaming at me if you're talking normally," she says. "I can't process questions very well. I act twitchy and weird, and it seemed to get worse with perimenopause."

She says her behaviour became a "nightmare" for her team. Pressed for an example, she explains: "If you asked me whether I wanted still or sparkling water, I'd say, 'That's a question, and I can't answer questions right now'.

Well, it's not exactly Mariah Carey demanding baskets of puppies and forbidding eye contact, but Imbruglia was shaken up.

The day after one concert, she told her co-writers David Sneddon and Anu Pillai, "Guys, I think I'm going to have to quit my job because I can't cope with how I'm treating people before the show."

They helped to talk her down, putting her fight-or-flight instincts into context.

"What they helped me realise is that I was trying to stop the behaviour with willpower, and if I just relaxed into it and said to myself, 'You know, you're about to perform in front of a lot of people, it's natural that you're nervous', maybe I wouldn't be resisting it as much."

The impromptu therapy session inspired a new song, Upside Down - but Imbruglia is understandably frustrated that perimenopause isn't more widely understood, saying many women are rejected by their GP when they seek HRT treatment.

"My mum never talked to me about it," she reflects, "but looking back, I know she had a really bad one.

"Her anxiety was off the charts, too, and I have a lot more compassion now, because she had four kids. I've only got one."

As a child in Sydney, Imbruglia was drawn to performing. She'd squeeze lemon on her hair to make it blonder, and put on concerts of Whitney Houston covers for her neighbours.

Before long, she was cast in commercials for Coca-Cola and Twisties, and spent her Christmases singing carols in shopping centres.

"But when you turn 15 or 16, and you're into boys, you're like, 'Oh, that's really naff. I don't want to be doing that any more'," she laughs.

From that point onwards, Imbruglia became "basically unparentable".

"I was sneaking out and sleeping in someone's car on the beach, then getting busted.

"My parents were really strict - and my mum would turn up at parties with my picture, going, 'Have you seen this girl?'

Music continued to be her solace. Dating a drummer, she switched allegiance from Whitney Houston to Tom Waits and Tori Amos, but the urge to sing remained.

You can see that hunger in a recently rediscovered photograph of a pre-fame Imbruglia , pressed up against the barriers of an INXS concert in 1992.

"It was my first ever concert," she says. "I was 15. I had white, tight jeans on."

In the photo, "everyone else is screaming but I'm looking at (Michael Hutchence) with this determination in my eyes.

"I'm studying him, like, 'How can I be up there too?'"

She got her chance in 1997 after quitting her role as builder's apprentice Beth Brennan in Aussie soap Neighbours.

Moving to London, she signed a deal with RCA Records and immediately scored an international hit with her first single, Torn.

Famously, the song was a cover – a fact journalists never let her forget, even though she co-wrote every other track on her debut album, Left of the Middle (lifetime sales, seven million copies).

"Yeah, I got famous on a song that I didn't write," she says now, "but there's more to what you bring to a song than whether you wrote the lyrics."

She still loves the song – "Torn was a beautiful gift" – but the furore around it fuelled her insecurities.

As a result, she essentially self-sabotaged her career. The lead single from her second album, That Day, was a free-verse stream-of-consciousness that sounded like a manic inner monologue.

"That was my rebellion against Torn," she says. "It doesn't have a chorus.

"That was my way of going, 'Can I get on with my life now? I've just started learning the craft of songwriting, I'm young, I didn't ask for this'."

In the midst of the madness, she auditioned for the lead role of Satine in Baz Luhrmann's Moulin Rouge – which counts as one of the stranger experiences of her career.

"The audition was, pretty much, 'Have an orgasm'," she grimaces. "Because I think that happens in the movie." (Indeed, Satine delivers a breathy boudoir monologue as she tries to seduce Ewan McGregor's character, Christian.)

But Imbruglia stresses it wasn't a creepy casting couch situation.

"It's Baz, that doesn't really fit," she says of the soft-hearted director.

"But I remember leaving and feeling really icky. Like, 'Ohhh, that was awful. Where's my mummy?'"

Back in the world of music, Imbruglia returned to more commercial sounds on hits like Wrong Impression (2002) and Shiver (2005). But sales dwindled and her fourth album was shelved by her label.

In the years that followed, she joined the Australian version of The X Factor and appeared in a UK production of Alan Ayckbourn's play Things We Do for Love, before making a tentative return to music with covers album Male (2015); and the more personal, introspective Firebird (2021).

"It was quitting music and coming back to it that gave me an appreciation of my abilities," she says.

"I might not be the best songwriter, even now, but there's only one me, and when I go inside myself and feel the emotion of what I'm writing about and deliver it, that's what my fans resonate with, and that's enough."

She certainly has a lot to say on Algorithm. As well as the frank discussion of mental health, the title track talks about her flirtation with internet conspiracy theories.

She won't say which ones ("I think it's irresponsible") but stresses the danger is omnipresent.

"There's a voice in my head that says, 'You don't want to click on that', and I'll click on it. It's like this compulsion.

"You have to change the settings. Don't allow yourself to be in a situation where your stress relief is scrolling on a phone in bed. It's just not healthy."

Ultimately, however, the album ends on a note of positivity.

Beautiful Love , co-written with Snow Patrol's Gary Lightbody, is a soaring hymn to embracing your flaws and making peace with life's highs and lows.

"I've always made the joke that I'll never be a Buddhist because it's a middle path," she smiles.

"I like the pendulum to swing. Whether it's extreme joy or extreme pain, I like to feel the experience of life."

articles.title: Hurricane Lowell threatens Hawaiian islands with life-threatening surf
articles.summary: Hurricane Lowell is expected to create life-threatening conditions even as it’s forecast to sidestep the major Hawaiian islands west of the archipelago by Monday night.
articles.body: Hurricane Lowell is expected to create life-threatening conditions even as it’s forecast to sidestep the major Hawaiian islands west of the archipelago by Monday night. It could remain a major hurricane — those with 111 mph or greater sustained winds — and is likely to create mudslides, as much as 10 inches of rain in Kauai, and life-threatening waves for parts of the island chain, the National Hurricane Center said. The tropical cyclone reached Category 5, defined by sustained winds of 157 mph or greater, overnight Friday before losing some of its steam and settling into Category 4’s limits of sustained winds of 130 to 156 mph by Saturday. Lowell appeared to be turning to the west-northwest Saturday, with the hurricane center saying this will likely trigger storm watch notices and other storm-related alerts for Kauai County and the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument. It was about 640 miles south-southwest of Honolulu, headed west-northwest at 7 mph, the hurricane center said, and was pushing out sustained winds of 145 mph. The hurricane center’s forecast cone has Lowell passing just west of the islands, from south to north, on Monday night. “Just because we’re on the edge of the cone doesn’t mean we’re safe,” John Bravender, warning coordination meteorologist at the National Weather Service, said at a Friday news conference. Maui could record up to 8 inches of rain, the National Hurricane Center said, but officials in the state are also focused on the storm’s impacts on the island of Kauai. “We are taking Hurricane Lowell extremely seriously and preparing now, before conditions deteriorate,” Gov. Josh Green said in a statement Friday. “I urge everyone, especially those in Kauaʻi County, to complete their preparations, follow official alerts and stay away from floodwaters, dangerous surf and other hazardous areas.” The governor’s office said the state was securing its harbors, deploying emergency personnel to strategic locations and monitoring dams for any possible breaches or overflows. Parts of Oahu and the Big Island were hit with intense flooding and strong winds from Tropical Storm Lala last month. Lowell is joined by two other tropical cyclones spinning in the northern half of the Pacific this week: Karina, a former Category 4 hurricane spinning about 755 miles east-northeast of Hilo, Hawaii, and Tropical Storm Marie, churning about 705 miles west of the southern tip of Baja California. Marie could produce high surf for Southern California during the holiday weekend, National Hurricane Center meteorologists said. The trio is part of a Northeast Pacific hurricane season that includes 15 named storms to date, according to Colorado State University. The high number is likely boosted by unusually warm water and the presence of an El Niño weather phenomenon with potentially historic rain for California, experts have said. Daniel Gilford, a meteorologist and atmospheric scientist at the nonprofit research group Climate Central, said El Niño’s warm sea surface temperatures are fueling potent tropical cyclones ahead of fall. “If we have extra fuel, we can push the accelerator down more and these storms can become more intense as a result,” he told NBC News. The phenomenon has been changing as a result of global warming, earth scientists have said, with United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres saying Thursday that El Niño is “being supersized before our eyes.” It’s a call to action, he said, to address climate change.

articles.title: Netanyahu boasts about bombing Qatar, says Gaza funds used for aid
articles.summary: Israeli PM says money he facilitated Qatar in sending to Gaza was recommended by Israeli security agencies.
articles.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has boasted about bombing Qatar, while dismissing domestic accusations that funds sent to Gaza were used for anything other than aid.

In an interview with Israel’s i24NEWS that he shared on social media on Saturday, Netanyahu said Qatar was a “hostile” state that did not dictate Israeli policy during its genocidal war on Gaza.

“I attacked Qatar, I also bombed it and attacked them during the war, and they attacked me,” Netanyahu boasted.

The interview comes just days before the one-year anniversary of Israel’s September 9, 2025, strike on Doha. The bombing killed five Hamas members and a Qatari security officer during a meeting to discuss the United States-backed Gaza ceasefire proposal.

Qatar, which has long served as a mediator in Middle East conflicts and beyond, has hosted Hamas’s political office since 2012, after what it says were requests from the US.

Doha condemned the strike as a “blatant violation of all international laws and norms”, with Qatari Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Majed al-Ansari calling it a “cowardly” assault.

Several countries in the region, including Iran and Pakistan, also condemned the attack, with leaders from Jordan, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia visiting Qatar shortly afterwards in a show of solidarity.

United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called the strikes a “flagrant violation” of Qatar’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

During a meeting later that month at the White House, Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump called Qatar’s Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani to apologise for the strike.

During the i24NEWS interview, Netanyahu also defended the transfer of millions of dollars in Qatari funds to Gaza that Israel had facilitated, saying the funds were intended for humanitarian purposes and had been transferred on the recommendation of Israeli security agencies Mossad and Shin Bet.

“All this money is worth 2 percent – 2 percent of all the money that entered the Strip,” the prime minister said.

Some of Netanyahu’s detractors have alleged that the funds were used to help Hamas prepare its October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, which precipitated its genocidal war on Gaza.

Qatar denies such allegations, saying any claims that it funds Hamas are unfounded and pointing to the strict oversight governing its aid transfers.

“Today, when they [Israel] are claiming that this is the financing of Qatar to Hamas, it has no basis,” Sheikh Mohammed said during last year’s Doha Forum.

“All our aid … went to Gaza, went to the people, and was under a very transparent process that the United States is fully aware about.”

Netanyahu made the remarks weeks before Israelis head to the polls on October 27, in the country’s first general election since its war on Gaza began in 2023.

With the October vote approaching, Netanyahu faces mounting pressure at home over his government’s handling of the Gaza war, the economy and the war with Iran — all shaping up as central issues in the campaign.

Analysts and critics say Netanyahu has repeatedly stoked tensions with other states ahead of elections to rally nationalist support.

articles.title: Russia calls talks with US envoys “useful”
articles.summary: A Russian aide said talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and two United States envoys were “highly useful” as the Americans attempt to restart stalled peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine. Yuri Ushakov, a foreign-policy adviser to Putin, said that U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner “outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues…
articles.body:
A Russian aide said talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and two United States envoys were “highly useful” as the Americans attempt to restart stalled peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine.

Yuri Ushakov, a foreign-policy adviser to Putin, said that U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner “outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement” but declined to share details on these plans, according to Reuters .

“The talks went beyond a mere exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis. Economic issues and ​potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in some detail,” Ushakov said.

The closed-door meeting – which lasted for over three hours – followed Putin authorizing a 72-hour pause on strikes against Kyiv to allow for the U.S. envoys’ safe travel, according to Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky similarly said that after speaking with Witkoff and Kushner, the country was “ready to observe a ceasefire in airstrikes” in cities where negotiations were taking place. He added the pause in strikes would start now with a planned end on Monday.

This weekend marks the first time traveling to Kyiv for negotiations for both envoys.

President Trump has remained optimistic about the meetings, telling reporters in the Oval Office Friday the two men are “bringing with them a proposal to end the war,” though he did not elaborate on what the plan entailed.

The yearslong dispute between Russia and Ukraine intensified following the last U.S.-facilitated meetings in February. Moscow has initiated near-continuous attacks in and around Kyiv for over a week, hitting buildings, warehouses and the central headquarters for Ukraine’s security service.

Zelensky reported that ahead of the U.S. envoys’ visit, two airports located 300 miles east of Kyiv were also hit by Russian airstrikes – killing four people and injuring five others.

Ukraine hit back throughout August with long-range attacks on oil storage and refining facilities in Russia including strikes on logistics hubs of online retailer Wildberries which has unsettled Russians living far from the front and hurt small businesses.

articles.title: U.N. General Assembly endorses a new world map that shows Africa’s size more accurately
articles.summary: The United Nations General Assembly on Friday endorsed a new world map that represents Africa more accurately in its larger size, a culmination of a recent campaign led by African countries and advocacy groups.
articles.body: The United Nations General Assembly on Friday endorsed a new world map that represents Africa more accurately in its larger size, a culmination of a recent campaign led by African countries and advocacy groups. Friday’s resolution, which was sponsored by Togo and backed by members of the African Union, was passed with 164 member states voting in favor. Only the U.S. voted against it while six other countries — Serbia, Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova and Ukraine — abstained. The vote encourages governments and institutions around the world to replace the traditional Mercator map, commonly used since the 16th Century, with the Equal Earth projection that advocates and geographers say shows locations more accurately. The Mercator projection shows Greenland and Africa as appearing to be about the same size whereas in the Equal Earth projection that shows continents in their true proportions, Africa is 14 times larger than Greenland. Friday’s resolution does not ban the Mercator projection or impose a replacement, but only encourages the use of the Equal Earth projection, the U.N. said in its report. “Maps shape our understanding of the world,” the global body quoted Togo’s Foreign Minister Robert Dussey as saying before the vote. “They guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions.” Africa No Filter, one of the lead campaigners for the adoption of the new map, hailed the resolution, adding: “We want to see accurate maps in schools, textbooks, newsrooms, businesses and on the digital platforms billions of people use every day.” Other countries have urged the adoption of the Equal Earth map. “Changing the map obviously doesn’t change the world. But correcting a representation that distorts it is already an act of truth,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on X after the vote. The Mercator map was designed by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European navigators at sea, but advocates say it distorted landmasses by enlarging regions near the poles such as North America and Greenland while shrinking Africa and South America. The 2018 Equal Earth projection, on the other hand, follows the Earth’s curvature and shows continents in their true proportions. Geographers say the traditional map is only useful for navigation. “Outside of that very narrow navigation application, there is no point in using it,” according to Mark Monmonier, a Syracuse University professor of geography.

articles.title: ‘There was no proper mobile network near our home’: These two Odisha sisters climbed hilltops to study, cleared NEET 2026 together without coaching
articles.summary: No internet at home, no expensive coaching and limited family income- but two sisters from a remote village in Odisha refused to let any of it come in.
articles.body: No internet at home, no expensive coaching and limited family income- but two sisters from a remote village in Odisha refused to let any of it come in the way of their dream of becoming doctors.Yajnaseni and her younger sister Dibyaseni, residents of Mahulapankha village in the Mayurbhanj district, have cleared the NEET 2026 after preparing largely through self-study and online classes. Their unusual preparation involved travelling away from home and climbing nearby hilltops whenever they needed a stronger mobile network.According to a report by Odisha TV, the sisters come from a financially struggling family. Their father, Gouranga Khatua, is a farmer, while their mother, Sunita, works as an Anganwadi helper. With the family's limited income, paying for private NEET coaching was not an option. But the lack of coaching did not mean the sisters stopped preparing.When the classroom was a hilltopFor many NEET aspirants, preparation means classrooms, coaching centres, test series and uninterrupted access to online study material. For Yajnaseni and Dibyaseni, even something as basic as an internet connection could not be taken for granted.The sisters relied mainly on online classes and self-study. However, poor mobile connectivity in their village frequently disrupted their access to online lessons. So, whenever they needed a stable network, they would leave home and climb nearby hilltops to study.Speaking to Kanak News, the sisters recalled, ““There was no proper mobile network near our home. We would go to the hill to study when we needed the internet. Sometimes, we even studied on the phone until midnight.”It was an inconvenient arrangement, but it allowed them to continue accessing the educational resources they could not otherwise afford. The sisters turned the lack of basic facilities into a challenge they were determined to overcome. Their story is less about a single moment of success and more about the daily effort required to keep studying when the usual support systems were missing.One succeeded on her third attempt, the other on her firstThe sisters' journeys to NEET success were not identical. Yajnaseni cleared the medical entrance examination on her third attempt, while her younger sister Dibyaseni succeeded in her first attempt, according to Odisha TV.Speaking about her preparation, Dibyaseni told Kanak News, “There was very little guidance available to me. My elder sister was my biggest guide and she guided me throughout.”For Yajnaseni, the third attempt eventually brought the breakthrough. For Dibyaseni, the first attempt was enough. Together, however, their results have given the family a reason to celebrate and brought them closer to their shared ambition of pursuing medical education.Parents supported them despite limited meansBehind the sisters' preparation was a family that had to make difficult financial choices. Their father earns through farming, while their mother works as an Anganwadi helper. The family's income has to meet household expenses as well as support the education of their daughters.Despite those limitations, their parents continued to support their studies. The sisters' achievement has now turned what could have been a story of deprivation into one of perseverance. For Yajnaseni and Dibyaseni, that improvisation meant taking their books and phones to the hills.More than a NEET resultClearing NEET is only the beginning for the sisters. The examination has opened the door to medical education, but their journey ahead will bring its own challenges.Still, their story offers a striking reminder that academic preparation does not always happen inside a coaching classroom. Sometimes it happens wherever a student can find a little time, a textbook and, in their case, a mobile signal.The sisters' achievement is particularly striking because they did not have the conventional advantages associated with NEET preparation. They had neither private coaching nor reliable internet access at home. What they did have was access to study material when they could find a network, the support of their parents and the determination to keep going.Their journey from a village with poor connectivity to clearing one of India's most competitive medical entrance examinations is therefore not simply a story about two students cracking NEET. It is also a story about how students in India's rural hinterland continue to find their own ways around the barriers between them and their ambitions.And for these two sisters, sometimes the road to becoming doctors began with a climb up a hill. The sisters told Kanak News that their aim is not just to become doctors but also to serve people who need medical care.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: Nearly 9,000 killed in Israeli attacks on Lebanon since 2023
articles.summary: More than 179 attacks on ambulance crews recorded since March 2, killing 179 healthcare workers.
articles.body:
The death toll from Israeli attacks on Lebanon over the past three years has exceeded 8,900, while the number of injured has reached nearly 30,600, according to Lebanese health authorities.

Israeli attacks from October 2023 to September 2026 killed 8,920 people and injured 30,595 others, the Lebanese Ministry of Public Health said in a statement on Saturday.

The numbers included 4,358 deaths and 12,359 injuries recorded since March 2.

A report published by the Health Ministry on Wednesday also said that there had been 179 Israeli attacks on ambulance crews since March 2, killing 135 healthcare workers.

The date marked Israel’s latest intensification of its war on Lebanon. On that day, an Israeli strike on Beirut killed 31 people following a Hezbollah rocket that targeted northern Israel.

According to the UNHCR, the United Nations refugee agency, 360,000 people remained displaced by Israeli aggression in August, including at least 22,000 living in collective shelters.

The figures came amid escalating Israeli violence across southern Lebanon despite two US-brokered “peace” agreements, both signed in June.

Israel has maintained its military occupation of southern Lebanon since March, when it announced it was installing a “buffer” zone. The June 26 framework agreement was contingent on Hezbollah’s disarmament.

Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem rejected the framework agreement, calling it “null and void”, demanding that Israel first end its occupation. The agreement did not specifically call for the withdrawal of Israeli forces in southern Lebanon.

On Friday, an Israeli air strike on Kfar Reman , a town in southern Lebanon, killed three people and injured 23 others. The Israeli military claimed it cleared Hezbollah fighters in tunnels under the strategic Ali al-Taher bridge.

Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency (NNA) also reported on Friday that Israeli raids and artillery shelling targeted seven towns in the Tyre and Nabatieh districts. There were no reported casualties.

Early on Sunday, Israeli warplanes bombed Zawtar al-Sharqiyah in southern Lebanon.

articles.title: Indonesia’s main airport suspends flights due to Anak Krakatau eruption
articles.summary: Volcanic ash from Mount Anak Krakatau disrupts flights at Soekarno-Hatta International airport, near Jakarta.
articles.body:
Flights have been suspended at Indonesia’s main airport outside Jakarta after volcanic ash from the erupting Mount Anak Krakatau was detected over the country’s capital.

Indonesia’s Soekarno-Hatta International airport said on Sunday morning that it suspended flight operations until 1:30pm local time (06:30 GMT) due to “increased eruptive activity” of the volcano, more than 150km (93 miles) away.

Anak Krakatau, which began erupting late on Friday, produced a fountain of lava and booming sounds that could be heard up to 700km (435 miles) away, according to the meteorological agency BMKG.

Two new eruptions were recorded on Sunday, the volcanology agency warned.

Ash was identified as high as 6,000 metres (20,000 feet) on the Java side of the volcano, and a plume of up to 15,000 metres (50,000 ft) on the Sumatra side and some parts of Banten province in Java, BMKG posted on its website.

An earlier airport suspension had been due to end at 5:30am (22:30 GMT Saturday), affecting 33 flights, including 16 international cancellations and seven delays, Indonesia’s Ministry of Transportation said.

Director General of Civil Aviation Lukman F Laisa said the extended suspension followed a “paper test” conducted between 12:35am and 1:05am (17:35 GMT and 18:05 GMT Saturday) that confirmed the presence of volcanic ash at the airport.

“Safety remains the top priority in every operational decision, including flight schedule adjustments made by airlines,” Lukman said, adding that authorities would continue monitoring the situation with airlines, air navigation services and Indonesia’s meteorological agency.

Singapore Airlines was among the carriers affected, cancelling two flights to and from Jakarta on Saturday and delaying two more into Sunday.

Indonesia’s disaster mitigation agency said on Saturday that there was no imminent tsunami risk from the eruption.

Anak Krakatau emerged from the sea in the 1920s in the caldera left by the catastrophic 1883 eruption of Krakatoa, one of the deadliest volcanic events in recorded history.

The volcano has erupted periodically in the decades since, including a 2018 eruption that triggered a partial collapse of its crater and a tsunami that killed more than 400 people along the coasts of Java and Sumatra.

Volcanic ash poses a serious hazard to aircraft, capable of damaging jet engines and reducing visibility.

articles.title: Hurricane Lowell holds Category 4 strength as Hawaii braces for a close call
articles.summary: US News: Powerful Hurricane Lowell remained a Category 4 storm with winds of up to 150 mph on Saturday as Hawaii braced for potentially dangerous impacts from .
articles.body: Powerful Hurricane Lowell remained a Category 4 storm with winds of up to 150 mph on Saturday as Hawaii braced for potentially dangerous impacts from the system, which is expected to turn sharply northwards and pass close to the western islands early next week.The storm, currently more than 600 miles south of Hawaii, has fluctuated between Category 4 and Category 5 strength in recent days. Forecasters said some additional intensification was possible over the next day or so before Lowell begins to weaken, but it is expected to remain near Category 4 strength as it approaches the island chain.The greatest uncertainty is how close Lowell will come to Niihau and Kauai. The National Hurricane Center's current forecast puts the storm's centre about 150 miles west of Niihau and 190 miles west of Kauai on Tuesday morning. However, forecasters said confidence in the exact track remains lower than normal.A shift of less than 100 miles eastwards could bring the major hurricane much closer to Hawaii, potentially producing more direct and severe impacts. Forecast models currently show outcomes ranging from a devastating landfall on Kauai or Oahu to a track more than 400 miles west of Niihau, which would bring relatively limited effects.Even without a major shift in the track, dangerous conditions are expected. Rough seas, coastal flooding and strong rip currents could affect the islands from as early as this weekend, with the western islands facing the greatest risk.The National Weather Service warned that major coastal flooding is possible in Kauai, while significant coastal flooding could also affect Oahu. Lowell is expected to generate large waves and push additional water towards Hawaii's southern shores, while tides are also forecast to be near their highest levels of the month, increasing the potential for flooding.Hawaii declares state of emergencyHawaii Gov. Josh Green declared a state of emergency across the entire state on Thursday, allowing authorities to mobilise resources and activate Hawaii National Guard units.Six high-water vehicles are being deployed to Kauai, while Kauai County has begun clearing drainage systems and positioning equipment in areas vulnerable to flooding. At least two state parks on the island have also closed camping facilities ahead of the storm.State land and natural resources crews were due to notify campers on Friday that they must leave immediately, according to the county. Authorities have also urged residents to maintain 14 days' worth of supplies.“Our state is still recovering from Lala, and we are not waiting for another storm to get close before preparing,” Green said in a news release.Green warned that the state could face further tropical systems in the coming weeks, describing the current period as a serious storm season.“This is a serious storm season,” Green said at a news conference Friday, noting his state is likely to face additional threatening tropical systems in the coming weeks.“We’ve got multiple storms because of El Niño that are stacking up – we’re told that’s what the fall is going to be like,” the governor said.Lowell's track remains uncertainLowell is forecast to turn sharply northwards this weekend after interacting with an area of low pressure high in the atmosphere north of Hawaii. The interaction is expected to pull the hurricane north, but the timing and strength of that interaction will determine how close the storm comes to the islands.Forecasters expect their confidence in Lowell's path to improve once the hurricane completes the turn.The storm's trajectory has drawn comparisons with Hurricane Iniki, which struck Kauai in 1992 as a Category 4 hurricane and remains Hawaii's worst storm on record.“We know that the memory of Hurricane ʻIniki is close to the surface for many of our families right now, so let us stay vigilant and prepare with a steady hand,” Kauai County Mayor Derek S.K. Kawakami said in a statement.He urged residents to remain patient, take care on the roads and check on their neighbours.“We don’t need any unforeseen tragedies while everyone is preparing,” Kawakami said. “Also, use this time to prepare and talk story with your ʻohana tonight so everyone knows the plan.”On Oahu, officials have also urged residents to remain vigilant, although the current forecast suggests the island's capital and largest city faces less immediate risk.“We feel much better about where things stand for Oʻahu heading into this weekend, but we are going to stay vigilant until Lowell makes that turn and moves away from us,” Honolulu Mayor Rick Blangiardi said in a statement.Third storm to threaten Hawaii in weeksLowell is the third tropical system to threaten Hawaii in roughly three weeks. Hurricane Lala brought feet of rain to the Big Island in mid-August, triggering severe flooding and causing extensive damage in communities along the island's southern end.Tropical Storm Moke followed later in August. Although it brought rain to the Big Island, its weaker strength meant the impacts were considerably less severe.The succession of storms has raised concerns as El Niño strengthens activity across the Pacific hurricane season. For Hawaii, the immediate focus remains on Lowell and the uncertainty surrounding its eventual path.“We’re hopeful that it will miss us, but if it does what Iniki did in 1992 or even does anything close … we could see tragic consequences,” Green said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: German voters head to polls as far-right AfD party eyes historic state win
articles.summary: Saxony-Anhalt elections could see AfD become the first far-right party to take power at a state level since WWII.
articles.body:
Voters in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt will head to closely watched polls on Sunday that could see the Alternative for Germany (AfD) become the first far-right party to take power at a state level since World War II.

Recent surveys place AfD at 40 percent, ahead of the centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU) at 23 percent.

AfD has led comfortably in the polls for months and has a chance at winning an absolute majority if several smaller parties fail to clear the 5 percent threshold to enter the German parliament. The results, however, are not guaranteed.

A CDU-led administration under incumbent state premier Sven Schulze is the most likely outcome if the AfD does not win a majority.

Weeks ⁠of coalition talks could follow the vote, depending on which parties surpass the 5 percent minimum.

AfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund, who was previously a member of the CDU, predicted gaining an absolute majority that would lead the anti-establishment party to national victory in 2029. He was named “Germany’s most dangerous man” by the influential magazine Der Spiegel.

“It was the others who erected the firewalls,” he told German tabloid Bild. “If no one wants to work with us, then we’ll just have to do it alone.”

An absolute majority would allow AfD to bypass mainstream parties’ “firewall” noncooperation policy, which the far-right party has already done at the local level.

For the AfD, the Saxony-Anhalt ‌elections are ⁠a stepping stone towards its larger ambition: securing national power in the 2029 federal elections.

The CDU is led by deeply unpopular German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

At a local campaign rally in Lower Saxony a week before the election, Merz urged other politicians to engage with AfD more effectively.

“We must address the issues at hand. We must also address our choice of words,” Merz said, referring to a statement by the AfD’s state leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Martin Reichardt.

Reichardt previously told the AfD’s youth organisation that Germany had become “a lazy, anti-social bum reeking of dope”.

Thousands of demonstrators gathered for a festival in support of democracy the night before the crucial election. Rally organisers estimated that between 15,000 and 20,000 people attended the demonstration.

Initial results are expected at about 16:00 GMT (6pm local time) on Sunday.

articles.title: South Africa’s chrome riches fuel a deadly underground economy
articles.summary: Behind South Africa’s chrome riches lies a shadow economy where migrants and unemployed workers face deadly conditions.
articles.body:
Rustenburg, South Africa – On August 13, a wall of soil collapsed and killed 14 miners, most of whom were believed to be undocumented migrants, at a disused mining site near Nkaneng, an informal settlement outside Rustenburg in South Africa’s mineral-rich North West province.

“It happened in a flash, and the earth swallowed a dozen,” Lerothodi Nale*, a migrant from Lesotho who escaped the collapse and ran to alert nearby security guards, told Al Jazeera.

Without a passport, Nale left the scene afterwards, fearing arrest. More miners could still be trapped underground, North West police commissioner Lieutenant-General Arthur Adams told journalists, including Al Jazeera.

The disaster has exposed a darker side of South Africa’s chrome wealth: an underground economy where vulnerable migrants, unemployed former mineworker and criminal groups converge around a lucrative mineral trade.

Rustenburg sits above the Bushveld Igneous Complex, one of the world’s richest geological formations, containing vast deposits of platinum-group metals and chrome. The region’s minerals have long powered industries including stainless steel production and advanced industrial applications.

South Africa is the world’s largest chrome producer and exporter, with much of its ore feeding global supply chains, particularly China’s stainless steel industry.

But alongside the formal mining sector, illegal extraction has expanded in parts of the country, including North West province, where authorities have raised concerns about unauthorised mining operations, environmental destruction and criminal groups exploiting abandoned and inactive mine sites.

For migrants like Nale, these abandoned pits offer both opportunity and danger.

“The disused mines are sitting graves with no geologists to confirm if rocks are still stable down there,” said metals governance expert Tapuwa Nhachi.

South Africa’s government has announced programmes to rehabilitate abandoned mines and close dangerous shafts, but critics say the scale of the response remains far below the challenge facing the country. Thousands of abandoned mine shafts remain across South Africa, creating opportunities for illegal operators and exposing workers to deadly conditions.

“Not a month goes without fatalities in abandoned mine holes,” Nhachi told Al Jazeera.

Chrome is attractive to illegal operators because deposits can often be reached closer to the surface, lowering extraction costs compared with deeper underground mining.

“For criminal networks, it becomes easier to extract, process and move the ore into supply chains,” environmental remediation expert Shamiso Mupara told Al Jazeera.

The result is an economy where profits are concentrated among those controlling equipment, transport routes and access to buyers, while miners take the greatest risks.

Nale describes a system that begins far beyond South Africa’s borders.

Undocumented migrants from Lesotho, Zimbabwe and Mozambique, alongside unemployed South Africans including former mineworker, are recruited by intermediaries who provide transport money and promise work around Rustenburg’s chrome fields.

On arrival, Nale said, workers are divided into groups controlled by criminal networks that provide food, mining equipment and, he alleges, explosives before sending them underground.

“At this juncture, we are held hostage by the alleged Maresha cartel, which, he says, takes 70 percent of our earnings and forces us to work in unsafe mines until we repay debts,” he said.

Nale alleges that miners can be transferred between groups and forced to continue working underground until additional ore is extracted.

The existence and scale of individual criminal groups involved in illegal mining are difficult to independently verify, but South African authorities have repeatedly linked illegal mining to organised crime, including violence, weapons trafficking and illicit financial networks.

Loren Landau, a migration expert at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, said the combination of poverty, unemployment and weak enforcement has created a steady supply of vulnerable workers.

“The pipeline sending scores of young male migrants to subterranean death does not pause because there are few viable job options left,” he told Al Jazeera.

“As soon as this batch of miners dies or gets injured, more destitute men are on the bus to replace them.”

At the gates of Marikana police station, which serves Nkaneng, Dineo Motho, 29, waited for news about her husband, Kgadi Ntuli, 35, who remained missing after the collapse.

Wrapped in a traditional Lesotho blanket against the winter cold, she had travelled about 400 kilometres (250 miles) overnight to South Africa after hearing about the disaster.

“He left home in January to try his luck in Rustenburg chrome pits because with drying lands in Lesotho, there was no water to nourish our goats, crops or fruits. There were no jobs, no food,” she told Al Jazeera.

Ntuli had been travelling between Lesotho and South Africa’s chrome fields, she said, earning enough money to support the family.

Her greatest hope was that he was among those who survived the collapse, but fled afterwards to avoid arrest.

For families like hers, survival itself can mean disappearing from authorities.

Economic hardship and worsening environmental pressures in parts of Southern African have increased vulnerability, pushing some people towards dangerous informal work.

The consequences are increasingly visible in communities surrounding South Africa’s mining zones.

Mmanotshe Ramokoka, traditional leader of the Baphalane Traditional Council in North West province, said illegal mining has damaged farmland, threatened water supplies and created conflict between communities and criminal groups.

“It’s an ecological warzone,” he told Al Jazeera.

He said illegal processing sites have appeared near farming areas, with open pits endangering livestock and waste affecting local environments.

“The gangs have millions to rent industrial equipment for stripping soil for chrome. Migrant diggers die for a tiny fraction of the profit,” Ramokoka said.

For years, illegal mining in South Africa was associated mainly with abandoned gold mines around Gauteng province, where informal miners known as zama zamas operated in old underground shafts.

But some experts and community leaders say pressure from the government’s Operation Vala Umgodi (“seal the mine holes” in isiZulu), launched in 2023 to target illegal mining, has encouraged some criminal operators to adapt and seek opportunities elsewhere. Authorities have described the operation as a nationwide effort to combat illegal mining and associated criminal activity.

Some miners now appear to be moving towards less-monitored chrome-producing areas in North West province.

The police have rejected allegations of widespread complicity and say they are taking action against illegal mining networks.

In a statement to media outlets including Al Jazeera, Lieutenant-Colonel Tinyiko Mathebula of the Hawks, the South African Police Service’s specialised organised crime unit, said 23 illegal mining cases had been registered in the Rustenburg area over the past two years, with 63 accused charged.

He added that police had seized 20 trucks and 15 excavators linked to illegal mining activities.

But enforcement alone may not end the cycle.

As long as poverty pushes workers towards dangerous pits and criminal groups control access to chrome wealth, the cycle is likely to continue.

“Nothing scares the hungry,” Landau said.

*Nale changed his surname to speak freely and avoid possible arrest.
